title: What securities do FDIC-insured banks hold?
gist: Using FDIC quarterly banking profile data on FRED, mortgage-backed securities still dominate FDIC-insured banks' securities portfolios at 60.7% as of Q1 2026, with Treasuries at 33.5%, munis at 5.8% and equities at 0.0%. Since 2008 the mix has rotated out of MBS and into Treasuries and munis, and since 2010 the held-to-maturity share of investment securities has climbed to 39.8% — changes Kansas City Fed researchers attribute to regulation, risk preferences, and a desire to shield mandatory capital levels from market-value swings.

insights.claim: As of Q1 2026, mortgage-backed securities account for 60.7% of the securities held by FDIC-insured institutions, followed by U.S. Treasury securities at 33.5%, state and municipal securities at 5.8%, and equity securities at 0.0%.
insights.speaker: St. Louis Fed — FRED Blog
insights.so_what: Sets the baseline exposure map for US bank balance sheets: agency MBS spread and duration risk, not corporate credit or equity, is the dominant securities risk in the banking system.

insights.claim: Mortgage-backed securities have consistently been the largest single securities holding of FDIC-insured institutions across the entire 1984-Q1 to 2026-Q1 record shown on FRED.
insights.speaker: St. Louis Fed — FRED Blog
insights.so_what: Four decades of persistence means bank demand for agency MBS is structural, not cyclical — a standing bid that policy shocks to the mortgage market transmit straight into bank capital.
insights.quote: We can see that mortgage-backed securities consistently represent the lion’s share of assets.

insights.claim: Equity securities are effectively absent from FDIC-insured banks' portfolios, rounding to 0.0% of holdings.
insights.speaker: St. Louis Fed — FRED Blog
insights.so_what: Equity drawdowns hit US banks through lending, fees and collateral channels rather than direct portfolio marks — the securities book is a rates story, not an equity story.
insights.quote: Equity securities (purple area): shares of ownership in a corporation (0.0%)

insights.claim: Between 2008 and 2026, the MBS share of FDIC-insured banks' securities holdings declined while the shares of US Treasury and state and municipal securities rose.
insights.speaker: St. Louis Fed — FRED Blog
insights.so_what: A nearly two-decade rotation makes banks a steadier marginal buyer of Treasuries and munis and a relatively shrinking one for agency MBS — relevant to who absorbs supply in each market.
insights.quote: between 2008 and the time of this writing, the share of those securities has decreased while the share of US Treasury and state and municipal securities has increased

insights.claim: Kansas City Fed researchers attribute the post-2008 shift in bank securities composition to changes in the regulatory environment and to evolving preferences for risk.
insights.speaker: St. Louis Fed — FRED Blog
insights.so_what: If regulation is a driver, deregulation or changes to liquidity/capital treatment could partially reverse the rotation and revive bank demand for MBS.
insights.quote: Researchers at the Kansas City Fed point to changes in the regulatory environment and evolving preferences for risk to explain this changing mix.

insights.claim: Bank securities split into trading securities, held for short-term gains and typically a small share of total assets, and investment securities, which are the larger share and are reported on the balance sheet as either held to maturity (HTM) or available for sale (AFS).
insights.speaker: St. Louis Fed — FRED Blog
insights.so_what: The HTM/AFS label determines whether market-value losses flow through capital, so the classification split is the key lens for reading unrealized-loss risk on any bank's book.

insights.claim: Available-for-sale securities have made up the majority of FDIC-insured banks' investment securities since 1996, but the held-to-maturity share has been rising since 2010 and now stands at 39.8% of all investment assets.
insights.speaker: St. Louis Fed — FRED Blog
insights.so_what: Nearly 40% of the investment book sits in HTM, where losses are not marked through capital — a growing gap between reported capital and mark-to-market value that matters in any forced-sale or deposit-run scenario.
insights.quote: since 2010, the proportion of investment securities that banks intend to hold until expiration, or maturity, has increased. At the time of this writing, they amount to 39.8% of all investment assets.

insights.claim: Kansas City Fed researchers ascribe the rising held-to-maturity share to a bank strategy of better protecting the value of mandatory capital levels against financial risk.
insights.speaker: St. Louis Fed — FRED Blog
insights.so_what: HTM growth is a deliberate capital-shielding tactic rather than a view on rates — it means reported regulatory capital increasingly understates duration losses embedded in bank securities books.
